conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood and make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.  

I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes with you using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s a brief, 10-question check-in that looks at how you’ve been feeling—physically and emotionally—over the past seven days. It isn’t a test and it won’t label you; it simply helps us see where you might need extra care or resources. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell me you’re in danger of hurting yourself or someone else.  

We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words. If anything feels confusing or too much, just let me know and we can pause. Ready to begin?  

First question: Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[slow exhale]  
Honestly? I can laugh—like, if my husband sends me a silly meme or the baby makes one of those random milk-drunk faces—but it feels kind of… muted? I’ll smile for a second and then it just fades. Most of the time things that used to crack me up barely register. So I guess I’d say it’s been difficult.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, eyes on lap]  
I mean… I can still laugh a little, but it’s not the same. It feels kind of forced, like I’m doing it because I “should,” not because it comes naturally. Most days the funny side of things just feels far away.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[slow head-shake]  
Not really. I keep telling myself I should be excited about little outings—like meeting a friend for coffee or even just taking the stroller around the block—but when the time comes it feels… flat. I still go, and once I’m there I might have a moment that feels okay, but the looking-forward part barely happens anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[quiet voice, eyes welling]  
Yeah… I do that a lot. If he spits up more than usual, or won’t nap, or I can’t settle him fast enough, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong.” I know logically babies just cry and spit up, but I still think, “A better mom would know how to fix this.” It hits me several times a day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands]  
Pretty much all the time. My mind keeps spinning worst-case stuff—like what if he stops breathing in the night, or what if I trip on the stairs and drop him. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just pop in and I can’t shut them off for a while. I eventually calm myself, but then they come back later.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[presses palms together]  
Yes. Not full panic attacks, but I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing and I feel like I can’t get a deep breath. It passes in a few minutes, but it’s happened most days this week, and there’s nothing actually happening—just my body going into “something’s wrong” mode out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a shaky breath]  
Yeah… I feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. The laundry pile, the dishes, the never-ending feeds—it all feels ten times heavier than it should. I’ll sit on the couch with him asleep on me and just stare at the mess, thinking, “I’ll never catch up.” I’m managing, but it’s like walking through thick mud every step.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[eyes flick to the window, voice low]  
That’s been me the past few nights. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps circling through all the “what-ifs” and things I didn’t get done. It takes me over an hour to fall asleep, and then I wake up at two or three a.m. with my heart pounding about the baby. I eventually drift off again, but it’s broken and I wake up still tired.
I have felt sad or miserable

[nods slowly, eyes glassy]  
Most days, yeah. It’s like a gray cloud that follows me around. I can still smile at the baby or chat with my mom on the phone, but the underlying feeling is just… heavy and sad. It lifts for a little while, then settles back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[swallows hard, voice cracks]  
Twice this week. Yesterday I just sat in the nursery rocker after he finally went down, and the tears came out of nowhere. Same thing a few nights ago when my husband asked how my day was—suddenly I couldn’t stop. It’s not all-day sobbing, but when it hits, it feels like the dam just bursts.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[quiet, eyes fixed on hands]  
Yeah… it’s flashed through my mind a couple of times, like “what if I just disappeared.” I’ve never planned anything and I don’t want to die—I just want the pressure to stop. The thoughts come and go in seconds, but they scared me enough that I figured I should tell you.

<quote>I feel like I'm walking through thick mud</quote> is how you described the endless feeds, chores, and worries that have replaced the joy you expected in early motherhood. You shared that laughter feels forced, outings feel flat, and a constant <sym>gray cloud of sadness</sym> follows you, broken only by sudden <sym>tears</sym> or episodes of racing heart and breathlessness. Despite loving your baby, you blame yourself whenever he fusses, and intrusive thoughts of harm-both to you and by you-frighten you enough to seek help.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient can still laugh but describes it as forced and unnatural, indicating a clear reduction in spontaneous enjoyment—closest to "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>the patient's loss of anticipatory joy and persistent flat mood.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "several times a day" and attributes routine infant behaviors to personal maternal failure, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, intrusive worst-case thoughts occurring "pretty much all the time" with inability to shut them off, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, sudden episodes of racing heart and breathlessness with no trigger, happening most days this week, consistent with "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks and struggling more than usual, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to anxious rumination, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad most days with persistent heaviness and only brief relief</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two distinct crying episodes this week triggered without warning, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>"Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score ≥14 with Item 10 ≥1 mandates urgent referral per EPDS guidelines. You endorsed 9 of 10 items at the highest or second-highest level, meeting DSM-5 threshold for Major <med>Depressive Disorder</med> with Peripartum Onset (≥5 symptoms >2 weeks, onset during pregnancy or ≤4 weeks postpartum). Core features include daily <sym>depressed mood</sym>, markedly diminished interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym> and inappropriate guilt, <sym>recurrent thoughts of death</sym>, plus <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>insomnia</sym>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange same-day urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist
2. Discuss safety plan and remove potential means of self-harm; keep emergency numbers handy
3. Begin evidence-based treatment: individual CBT or IPT plus antidepressant compatible with breastfeeding as indicated
4. Schedule daily support check-ins (partner, family, or friend) and weekly professional follow-up
5. Prioritize rest: split-night feeds, accept household help, wind-down routine, limit screen time after feeds
6. Add calming strategies: paced breathing, 5-minute stroller walks, brief mindfulness while baby sleeps
7. Connect with local <med>PPD</med> support group or online peer forum; share feelings without judgment
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Self-report & behavioral observation, 10-item EPDS-style questionnaire

Symptoms / behavioral indicators endorsed  
- Marked anhedonia (reduced laughter, anticipatory enjoyment)  
- Persistent low mood, described as “gray cloud,” with tearfulness ≥2×/week  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt tied to infant-care perceived failures  
- Generalized anxiety & intrusive catastrophic worries re: infant safety  
- Episodic panic-style sensations (racing heart, breathlessness) most days  
- Overwhelm / “drowning” feeling re: routine tasks  
- Initial & middle insomnia related to rumination / anxiety  
- Passive self-harm ideation (“what if I just disappeared”) without plan or intent  

Pattern  
Consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum mood-anxiety spectrum presentation; functional impact evident (sleep disruption, task avoidance, distress).

Safety  
Presence of self-harm thoughts (passive) → elevated risk flag; further safety assessment warranted.

Screening impression  
High clinical concern for major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; exceeds threshold for routine follow-up and requires prompt mental-health evaluation and safety planning.
